chapters.title: Application architecture
chapters.subtitle: Apps, services, boundaries and ADRs
chapters.summary: Django gives you apps, models and views; it does not give you a domain architecture. Use services, selectors and explicit boundaries to keep a growing codebase changeable.
chapters.quick_answer: Keep views thin, models focused on data and invariants, and put multi-step use cases in a service function. Use selectors for read queries. Record consequential decisions as ADRs and enforce boundaries with imports and tests.

sections.title: App boundaries and the dependency rule
sections.body:
A Django app should own a coherent domain: billing, catalog, accounts. It should not import another app's internal modules freely. Depend on a small public surface (services, selectors, events), not on private helpers.

When two apps need the same utility, move it to a shared `common` app only if it is genuinely generic. A `utils.py` that imports everything is a new monolith.
sections.code:
billing/
  models.py
  services.py      # public use cases
  selectors.py     # public read queries
  gateways.py      # provider adapters
  tests/

catalog/
  models.py
  services.py
  selectors.py

# billing/services.py
def start_subscription(account, plan, gateway) -> Subscription: ...
sections.note: A public module is a promise. Rename/refactor it with the same care as an API endpoint.

sections.title: Services and selectors
sections.body:
A service is a write use case: it validates, changes state, emits side effects after commit and returns a result. A selector is a read query: it returns a queryset or a small DTO, already scoped and optimized.

Do not create a service for every model method. Create one when the operation spans models, transactions or external systems.
sections.note: Pass keyword-only arguments for services with several parameters. It makes call sites readable and refactors safer.

sections.title: DTOs and domain events
sections.body:
Returning ORM objects from every service couples callers to the schema. A small dataclass/DTO at a module boundary makes the contract explicit and testable.

Domain events (`OrderPlaced`, `InvoicePaid`) let other apps react without a direct import. An outbox makes the event reliable; an in-process signal is not a delivery guarantee.
sections.note: Do not turn every internal function into a DTO. Use them where a boundary is real.

sections.title: ADRs and fitness functions
sections.body:
An Architecture Decision Record captures context, decision, alternatives and consequences. Store it next to the code. A future maintainer needs to know why the team chose schema-per-tenant or a queue, not just what the code does.

Fitness functions are automated checks that enforce a boundary: no imports from `catalog` into `billing`, no queries in templates, no cross-tenant access. A lint rule or a test is stronger than a wiki page.
sections.note: Start with one or two fitness functions. A hundred rules will be disabled on day two.

sections.title: Dependency direction: views -> application -> domain
sections.body:
A useful Django architecture is a direction of dependencies, not a folder aesthetic:

- interface layer: views, serializers, forms, admin
- application layer: services, selectors, use-case functions
- domain layer: rules, value objects, policies
- infrastructure: ORM models, cache, email, storage, third-party clients

Dependencies point inward. A view may call a service; a service may use the ORM; the domain should not import a view, request or response. This keeps the rule testable without HTTP and prevents circular imports.

In a small app, a `services.py` and `selectors.py` are enough. Do not add a repository abstraction over the Django ORM just to look enterprise; add it when you need to swap a boundary or isolate a complex query. The point is to make the transaction and permission boundary explicit.

Name services after use cases (`place_order`, `invite_member`), not after tables (`order_service`).
sections.note: A service should own the transaction boundary and the side effects. The view should translate HTTP to inputs and the result to a response.

sections.title: Reliable side effects: on_commit, outbox and idempotency
sections.body:
If you send email or publish an event inside a transaction before it commits, the side effect can happen even when the database write rolls back. `transaction.on_commit(callback)` delays the callback until a successful commit, but it is not durable: a process crash after commit loses the callback.

For important side effects, write an outbox row in the same transaction and let a worker deliver it. The worker marks rows delivered and retries failures. This gives at-least-once delivery; the consumer must be idempotent.

Idempotency means repeating the same operation has the same effect. Use a unique idempotency key on the request or event, store the result, and return the stored result on a repeat. Do not rely on "the client will not retry"; networks retry.

Keep the outbox table small with a purge job, and give the worker a visibility timeout so a stuck row can be retried.
sections.note: `on_commit` is a good fit for cache invalidation and lightweight notifications. Durable business events belong in an outbox.
sections.code:
from django.db import models, transaction

class OutboxEvent(models.Model):
    topic = models.CharField(max_length=80)
    payload = models.JSONField()
    created_at = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)
    delivered_at = models.DateTimeField(null=True, blank=True)

def place_order(*, customer, sku, quantity):
    with transaction.atomic():
        order = Order.objects.create(customer=customer, sku=sku, quantity=quantity)
        OutboxEvent.objects.create(
            topic="order.created",
            payload={"order_id": order.pk, "sku": sku},
        )
    return order

# Worker: claim one undelivered row with a row lock, deliver,
# then set delivered_at. A retry is safe because the consumer
# deduplicates on (topic, payload["order_id"]).

pitfalls: A `utils.py` that imports every app and becomes impossible to test.
Putting multi-step use cases in views or model `save()`.
Returning ORM objects across every boundary.
Using signals as a reliable event bus.
Architecture documents that nobody updates.
checklist: Apps own coherent domains and expose a public surface.
Multi-step writes live in services.
Read queries live in selectors and are scoped.
Consequential decisions have ADRs.
At least one fitness function enforces a boundary.

chapters.title: Django internals
chapters.subtitle: App registry, request lifecycle, settings and checks
chapters.summary: What happens between `manage.py` and a response: app loading, settings, URL resolution, middleware, the view and the response. Knowing the order makes configuration bugs obvious.
chapters.quick_answer: Django populates the app registry, loads settings, builds the middleware chain, resolves the URL, calls the view and unwinds the response. `AppConfig.ready()` runs once during startup; use it for registration, not queries. System checks run before the server starts.

sections.title: Startup and the app registry
sections.body:
`django.setup()` configures settings, populates the app registry and imports each app's models. `AppConfig.ready()` runs after models are loaded. Importing models from `ready()` is safe; querying the database is not (the app may be starting before migrations run).

Signals should be connected in `ready()`, not at import time in `models.py`, to avoid double registration.
sections.code:
# catalog/apps.py
from django.apps import AppConfig

class CatalogConfig(AppConfig):
    default_auto_field = "django.db.models.BigAutoField"
    name = "catalog"

    def ready(self):
        from . import signals  # noqa: F401
sections.note: `default_auto_field` prevents a deprecation warning and keeps new models consistent.

sections.title: The request lifecycle
sections.body:
A request enters through WSGI/ASGI, passes the middleware chain, is matched by the URL resolver, dispatched to the view, and returns through the middleware in reverse. Exceptions can be handled by middleware or become a 404/500 response.

`request.resolver_match` is available after URL resolution. Middleware that runs before resolution cannot know the view name unless it resolves the path itself.

sections.title: The settings object
sections.body:
`settings` is a lazy object. Accessing a setting before `DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE` is configured raises `ImproperlyConfigured`. In scripts, set the environment variable and call `django.setup()` before importing app modules.

`override_settings` swaps values in tests. Some settings are read at import time; changing them after startup may not take effect.
sections.code:
import os
os.environ.setdefault("DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE", "config.settings")

import django
django.setup()

from django.conf import settings
print(settings.DATABASES["default"]["ENGINE"])
sections.note: Never import Django models before `django.setup()` in a standalone script.

sections.title: The system checks framework
sections.body:
`manage.py check` runs registered checks before the server starts. Django's own checks cover models, URLs, admin, security and deployment. You can register a custom check with `@register` and return `Error`, `Warning` or `Info`.

Use checks for configuration invariants: missing env vars, an invalid storage backend, a required middleware. Do not use them for database queries.
sections.note: Warnings are easy to ignore. Promote a check to `Error` only when the app genuinely cannot start.

sections.title: WSGI, ASGI and handler classes
sections.body:
`WSGIHandler` and `ASGIHandler` load middleware and the URLconf, then call the view. `get_wsgi_application()` / `get_asgi_application()` return the callable your server imports. They must run after settings are configured.

ASGI adds the lifespan protocol and long-lived connections. A WSGI-only server cannot serve WebSockets.
sections.code:
# config/wsgi.py
import os
from django.core.wsgi import get_wsgi_application
os.environ.setdefault("DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE", "config.settings")
application = get_wsgi_application()
sections.note: A server command references `config.wsgi:application`; a typo here is a startup failure, not a request error.

pitfalls: Querying the database in `AppConfig.ready()`.
Importing models before `django.setup()` in scripts.
Connecting signals twice by importing from `models.py`.
Assuming middleware knows the resolved view before URL resolution.
Using checks for slow queries or network calls.
checklist: Startup order is understood by the team.
`ready()` is side-effect-light.
Settings are configured before app imports.
Custom checks are fast and actionable.
WSGI/ASGI entry points match the server command.

chapters.title: Upgrading Django
chapters.subtitle: LTS cadence, deprecations and a safe upgrade
chapters.summary: Django ships feature releases every eight months and security patches for supported series. Upgrade deliberately: read the release notes, remove deprecations, test on the target version and keep a rollback path.
chapters.quick_answer: Stay on a supported patch. Read the release notes for every version you cross, fix deprecation warnings before the removal release, run the test suite on the target version, and deploy with a rollback plan. Never jump multiple major versions without reading each step.

sections.title: Release cadence and support
sections.body:
Django has feature releases roughly every eight months. Every third feature release is LTS. Security fixes land on supported feature releases and the current LTS. A version that is “working fine” can still be unsupported and unsafe.

Pin an exact version (`Django==6.1.2`) or a narrow range. Test the patch upgrade in CI; patch releases are intended to be drop-in but can change behaviour.

head: Series
Kind
Upgrade stance
rows: Long support; good default for conservative teams
Short support; upgrade before extended support ends
Current stable; read the release notes

sections.title: Deprecations and removed APIs
sections.body:
Django warns before removing an API. Run with warnings enabled and fix deprecations on the version before the removal. A deprecation warning is a scheduled breakage, not noise.

Common upgrade work: settings renamed/removed, `CheckConstraint.check` → `condition`, storage settings → `STORAGES`, `django.utils.timezone.utc` removal, `ugettext` → `gettext`, and third-party packages that lag.
sections.code:
python -W error::DeprecationWarning manage.py test
python manage.py check --deploy
sections.note: Turning every deprecation into an error can be noisy from dependencies. Scope the warning filter to your apps if needed.

sections.title: A safe upgrade process
sections.body:
1. Read the release notes and “backwards incompatible changes”.
2. Create a branch and upgrade the pin.
3. Run `pip check`, the full test suite and `makemigrations --check`.
4. Run the app in staging with production-like data.
5. Deploy with a rollback image and a database backup.
6. Watch error rates and latency after the deploy.
sections.code:
pip install -U "Django==6.1.2"
pip check
python manage.py check
python manage.py makemigrations --check --dry-run
python manage.py test
sections.note: A Django upgrade is also a dependency upgrade. Check django-stubs, DRF, Channels, Celery and storage backends.

sections.title: Compatibility and rollback
sections.body:
Third-party packages are the usual blocker. Check their supported Django versions before upgrading. If a package is unmaintained, replace it before it blocks a security patch.

A rollback plan includes the previous container image, a database backup and awareness of irreversible migrations. If a migration is destructive, keep the old column until the new version is proven.
sections.code:
# CI matrix
python -m pip install "Django~=5.2.0"
python manage.py test
python -m pip install "Django~=6.1.0"
python manage.py test
sections.note: Testing only the newest Django hides the LTS compatibility you promised. Test both if you support both.

pitfalls: Running an unsupported Django series with known CVEs.
Skipping release notes and discovering a removed API in production.
Upgrading Django without upgrading django-stubs/DRF/Channels.
No rollback image or database backup.
Treating deprecation warnings as harmless.
checklist: Django is on a supported patch.
Release notes for every crossed version were read.
Deprecations are fixed before removal.
Dependencies support the target Django.
Staging and rollback plans exist.

chapters.title: Feature flags
chapters.subtitle: Safe rollout, experiments and cleanup
chapters.summary: A feature flag separates deploy from release. Used well, it reduces risk; used badly, it creates a permanent maze of dead branches.
chapters.quick_answer: Store flags with an owner and expiry, evaluate them server-side, log exposure, and remove the flag after rollout. A kill switch is a flag with an operational owner; an experiment needs a hypothesis and a metric.

sections.title: A flag model that stays honest
sections.body:
At minimum: key, description, enabled, rollout percentage, allowed users/tenants, owner, created/expires. Evaluate deterministically per user (hash of user id + key) so a user does not flip between variants.

Cache the flag configuration, but invalidate on change. A flag service outage should fail closed or open according to the feature's risk.
sections.code:
class FeatureFlag(models.Model):
    key = models.SlugField(unique=True)
    description = models.TextField()
    enabled = models.BooleanField(default=False)
    rollout_percent = models.PositiveSmallIntegerField(default=0)
    owner = models.ForeignKey(settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL, on_delete=models.PROTECT)
    expires_on = models.DateField(null=True, blank=True)

def is_enabled(key, user):
    flag = cache.get_or_set(f"flag:{key}", lambda: FeatureFlag.objects.get(key=key), 60)
    if not flag.enabled:
        return False
    bucket = int(hashlib.sha256(f"{key}:{user.pk}".encode()).hexdigest(), 16) % 100
    return bucket < flag.rollout_percent
sections.note: A percentage rollout is not a random coin flip per request; it must be stable for the same user.

sections.title: Rollout and experiments
sections.body:
Roll out internally, then a small percentage, then everyone. Watch error rate, latency and the product metric at each step. A canary without a comparison metric is just a slower deploy.

An A/B experiment needs a hypothesis, a primary metric, a sample-size plan and a stop rule. Do not peek daily and stop when the graph looks good.
sections.note: Log the variant with the conversion event. Without exposure logging, the experiment cannot be analyzed.

sections.title: Cleanup is part of the feature
sections.body:
A flag that stays after 100% rollout is technical debt. Add an expiry date and a cleanup task. Remove the old branch, the flag checks and the flag row in one change.

Keep a small set of permanent operational kill switches (payments, signup, email) with owners and runbooks. Those are not experiments.
sections.code:
# Cleanup checklist
# 1. Flag at 100% for a full release cycle.
# 2. Remove the old code path.
# 3. Remove the flag checks and the database row.
# 4. Delete the experiment dashboard.
sections.note: A flag with no owner and no expiry is a permanent branch. Treat it as a bug.

pitfalls: Evaluating flags only on the client; users can bypass them.
Random per-request rollout that flips a user between variants.
No exposure logging, making experiments unanalyzable.
Flags that never expire.
A flag service outage taking down checkout.
checklist: Flags have owners and expiry dates.
Evaluation is server-side and deterministic.
Exposure is logged with the outcome metric.
Kill switches have runbooks.
Cleanup is scheduled.

chapters.title: Payments & webhooks
chapters.subtitle: Idempotency, signatures, state machines and reconciliation
chapters.summary: Payments are a distributed system with money. Treat provider webhooks as untrusted, retryable events, keep a local state machine and reconcile against the provider.
chapters.quick_answer: Verify the webhook signature, dedupe by provider event id, apply transitions through a state machine, and reconcile periodically. Use the provider's idempotency key for charges. Never trust an amount or status sent by the client.

sections.title: Idempotency is the core requirement
sections.body:
A network timeout does not mean the charge failed. Retrying without an idempotency key can charge twice. Generate a key per checkout attempt and persist it with the order; reuse it on retry.

The provider's event id is the dedupe key for webhooks. Store it before applying the event, ideally in the same transaction as the state change.
sections.note: Do not generate a new idempotency key on every retry; that defeats the purpose.

sections.title: Verify and dedupe webhooks
sections.body:
Verify the signature against the raw request body, not the parsed JSON. Reject stale timestamps to reduce replay. Return 2xx quickly and enqueue the processing; the provider will retry non-2xx and timeouts.

An endpoint that does slow work inline will time out and trigger duplicate deliveries. Idempotency makes the duplicates harmless.
sections.note: `csrf_exempt` is correct for a signature-verified webhook. The signature is the authentication.

sections.title: A payment state machine
sections.body:
Model the allowed transitions explicitly: `pending → authorized → captured → refunded`, with failure/dispute branches. Reject impossible transitions instead of overwriting status. Store provider ids and raw events for audit.

Status is not a boolean. A `paid` flag cannot represent partial refunds, disputes or delayed capture.
sections.note: Store money as `Decimal`, never `float`. Keep currency with the amount.

sections.title: Reconciliation and disputes
sections.body:
Webhooks can be missed. A daily reconciliation job fetches provider events or settlement reports and compares them with local payments. Alert on mismatches; do not silently “fix” them.

Refunds, chargebacks and disputes are part of the model. A refund is a new ledger entry, not a deletion of the original payment.
sections.note: Reconciliation is read-only until a human or a tested rule decides what to do with a mismatch.

pitfalls: Trusting a client-supplied amount or status.
Charging without an idempotency key.
Parsing the webhook body before verifying the signature.
Doing slow work inline and timing out the provider.
Using a boolean `paid` field for a complex lifecycle.
No reconciliation job.
checklist: Charges use a persisted idempotency key.
Webhook signatures are verified against the raw body.
Events are deduped by provider id.
Payment transitions are explicit.
A reconciliation job runs and alerts on mismatches.

chapters.title: HTMX with Django
chapters.subtitle: Partials, CSRF, out-of-band swaps and history
chapters.summary: HTMX keeps the HTML on the server and lets the browser request fragments. The Django work is small: detect the request, return the right partial, include CSRF and keep URLs/history coherent.
chapters.quick_answer: Render a full page for a normal request and a fragment for an `HX-Request`. Use `hx-target`/`hx-swap` deliberately, send CSRF via `hx-headers`, and use `hx-push-url` plus a full-page fallback for navigation.

sections.title: Full page vs partial
sections.body:
An HTMX request includes `HX-Request: true`. The view can return the same template with a different base or a dedicated fragment. Keep one source of truth for the fragment; do not duplicate markup.

A navigation link should still work without JavaScript. Progressive enhancement is the point.
sections.code:
def post_list(request): posts = Post.objects.filter(published=True).select_related("author") template = "blog/_post_list.html" if request.headers.get("HX-Request") else "blog/list.html" return render(request, template, {"posts": posts}) # template
{% include "blog/_post_list.html" %}
sections.note: A fragment endpoint is still a view. Apply the same permissions and query scoping as the full page.

sections.title: Forms and CSRF
sections.body:
HTMX submits normal forms. Include `{% csrf_token %}`; for a button with `hx-post`, add `hx-headers='{"X-CSRFToken": "{{ csrf_token }}"}'` or use a global `hx-headers` on `<body>`.

Return the form with errors and a 422/400 status when validation fails; HTMX swaps the response by default. Use `hx-target` to the form container so errors appear in place.
sections.code:
{% csrf_token %}
{{ form.as_p }}
sections.note: A 200 response with errors will still swap. Return 422 if your client code checks `HX-Reswap`/status.

sections.title: Out-of-band swaps and history
sections.body:
`hx-swap-oob` updates a second part of the page (a counter, a toast) in the same response. The OOB element must have a matching id. Use it sparingly; too many OOB updates make the response hard to reason about.

`hx-push-url` updates the address bar. The URL must return the full page on a direct load. `hx-boost` enhances links and forms while preserving normal navigation.
sections.code:
{{ cart_count }}
{{ product.name }}
sections.note: An OOB element that is missing from the page is silently ignored. Test the full page after a swap.

sections.title: Testing HTMX flows
sections.body:
Test both shapes: a normal request returns the full page, an `HX-Request` returns the fragment. Assert the fragment does not contain the full layout and that permissions still apply. Use a browser test for the swap/history behaviour.

A fragment endpoint that leaks another tenant's rows is a data breach, even if the UI never links to it.
sections.code:
def test_list_fragment(self):
    response = self.client.get("/blog/", HTTP_HX_REQUEST="true")
    self.assertTemplateUsed(response, "blog/_post_list.html")
    self.assertNotContains(response, "<html")
sections.note: Django's test client passes custom headers with the `HTTP_` prefix.

pitfalls: Duplicating fragment markup in full-page and partial templates.
Forgetting CSRF on `hx-post`.
Returning a full page for an HTMX request and swapping it into a div.
Pushing a URL that does not work on direct load.
Skipping permission checks on fragment endpoints.
checklist: Every HTMX endpoint works without JavaScript.
Fragments have a single source of truth.
CSRF is sent for unsafe methods.
Pushed URLs return full pages.
Fragment endpoints enforce permissions.

chapters.title: CSV, PDF & exports
chapters.subtitle: Streaming, formatting and large exports
chapters.summary: Exports are a data boundary: encode safely, stream instead of buffering, and move large jobs out of the request. CSV formula injection is a real vulnerability.
chapters.quick_answer: Stream CSV rows with `StreamingHttpResponse`, generate XLSX/PDF in a worker for large exports, set `Content-Disposition: attachment`, and escape cells that begin with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@` to prevent spreadsheet formula injection.

sections.title: Streaming CSV
sections.body:
`csv.writer` writing to a generator-backed response keeps memory flat. Batch the queryset with `.iterator(chunk_size=500)`. Include a header row and set the correct content type and filename.

Do not build the entire CSV in a list; a million rows will exhaust the worker.
sections.note: The `Echo` class adapts `csv.writer` to a streaming response. A normal `StringIO` buffers the whole file.

sections.title: CSV formula injection
sections.body:
Spreadsheets treat cells starting with `=`, `+`, `-` or `@` as formulas. A customer name like `=HYPERLINK(...)` can exfiltrate data or run commands when opened. Prefix dangerous cells with an apostrophe or a tab, and document the choice.

This is not a Django bug; it is a spreadsheet format hazard. Escape on export, not only on input.
sections.code:
DANGEROUS = ("=", "+", "-", "@", "\t", "\r")

def safe_cell(value):
    text = str(value)
    return "'" + text if text.startswith(DANGEROUS) else text
sections.note: Numbers that legitimately start with `-` need a product decision; escaping them changes the displayed value.

sections.title: XLSX and PDF
sections.body:
For XLSX, `openpyxl` can write a workbook to a `BytesIO` for small files. For large workbooks, use `write_only=True` or generate in a worker and store the result. For PDFs, render HTML with a headless browser or a library such as WeasyPrint; keep fonts and CSS self-contained.

A PDF generator is a CPU-heavy dependency. Run it outside the request if it takes more than a second or two.
sections.code:
from io import BytesIO
from openpyxl import Workbook
from django.http import HttpResponse

def export_xlsx(request):
    workbook = Workbook(write_only=True)
    sheet = workbook.create_sheet("Orders")
    sheet.append(["id", "total", "status"])
    for order in Order.objects.filter(owner=request.user).iterator(chunk_size=500):
        sheet.append([order.pk, float(order.total), order.status])
    buffer = BytesIO()
    workbook.save(buffer)
    response = HttpResponse(
        buffer.getvalue(),
        content_type="application/vnd.openxmlformats-officedocument.spreadsheetml.sheet",
    )
    response["Content-Disposition"] = 'attachment; filename="orders.xlsx"'
    return response
sections.note: `float(Decimal)` loses precision. For money, export a string or use a numeric cell with the correct number format.

sections.title: Large exports as a job
sections.body:
A 500k-row export should not occupy a web worker. Create an `ExportJob` row, enqueue a task, write the file to storage, and email or notify the user with a short-lived download link.

The job needs progress, failure state and cleanup. A stale export file is a data-retention issue.
sections.code:
@shared_task(bind=True)
def build_export(self, job_id):
    job = ExportJob.objects.get(pk=job_id)
    path = f"exports/{job.pk}.csv"
    with default_storage.open(path, "w") as handle:
        write_csv(handle, job.queryset())
    job.file.name = path
    job.status = "ready"
    job.save(update_fields=["file", "status"])
sections.note: Scope the export query to the requesting user/tenant and store that scope in the job, not in a global variable.

pitfalls: Building a huge CSV in memory.
Forgetting `Content-Disposition` and rendering the file in the browser.
Leaving CSV formula injection unescaped.
Running a multi-minute export in the request.
Exporting rows without tenant/user scoping.
checklist: Exports stream or run in a worker.
Filenames and content types are correct.
Formula-injection cells are escaped.
Export queries are scoped.
Old export files have a retention policy.
